q: What is the key difference between image classification and image segmentation?
options: Classification gives one label to the whole image, while segmentation labels every pixel
Classification labels each pixel, while segmentation labels the whole image once
Classification draws bounding boxes, while segmentation gives one class number
Classification needs a mask label, while segmentation needs a one hot vector
explain: Segmentation localises the target by assigning a class to every pixel. Classification only returns one label for the entire picture.

q: A photo shows a person and a small dog. Why is a single label such as DOG or HUMAN not enough?
options: A CNN cannot give a single label when two objects are present
A single label needs every image resized to a fixed shape
One label cannot show where objects are or how many there are
A single label needs the fully connected layers to be removed
explain: Classification cannot say where an object is or how many there are, and one label does not fit a scene with several objects. That is why methods that locate objects are needed.

q: Which statements about the labels used to train a segmentation network are correct?
options: Only the centre coordinates and the box size are required
The label is given as a binary mask image
The mask shows where the target object sits across the image
Producing ground truth masks is labour intensive
One categorical label is enough for the whole image
explain: Segmentation needs a mask for every training image, which takes a lot of effort. A single label or a box description would not give pixel level detail.

q: What should a segmentation network output for a given input image?
options: One class prediction for the whole image
A predicted mask image showing where the object is
A list of bounding boxes with confidence scores
A one hot vector with one entry per class
explain: Unlike a classifier, which gives one label, a segmentation network produces a prediction mask that localises the object. Boxes with confidence scores belong to object detection.

q: Which tasks need a class label for each pixel?
options: Giving one label to each photo in a holiday album
Analysing satellite images
Predicting whether an email is spam
Outlining a brain tumour in a scan
Understanding the road scene for a self driving car
explain: Segmentation suits tasks that need localisation, such as medical imaging, self driving cars and satellite analysis. Labelling whole photos is plain classification.

q: What are the three sections of a U-Net model?
options: Encoding blocks, a pooling layer and classification blocks
Convolution blocks, a dropout section and softmax blocks
Contraction blocks, a grid layer and anchor blocks
Contraction blocks, a bottleneck and expansion blocks
explain: U-Net shrinks the image in contraction blocks, passes through a bottleneck and then rebuilds an image in expansion blocks. The shape of this layout looks like a U.

q: Why does an expansion block of U-Net receive a copy and crop of feature maps from the matching contraction block?
options: To reduce the number of classes the network must predict
To remove duplicate bounding boxes from the output
To make up for information lost during max pooling
To convert the mask back into a single label
explain: Max pooling throws away detail on the way down. Copying and cropping the earlier feature maps hands some of that detail back so the reconstructed mask is sharper.

q: Which statements about U-Net are correct?
options: The bottleneck sits between the contraction and expansion blocks
It is trained with a single label per image
Its contraction blocks end with an up sampling layer
Expansion blocks use an up sampling layer
It converts the image into a feature vector and then reconstructs a segmented image
It outputs bounding boxes around each object
explain: U-Net encodes then rebuilds the image, with the bottleneck in the middle and up sampling in the expansion path. It outputs a mask, not boxes, and needs mask labels.

q: How does the output of object detection differ from the output of segmentation?
options: Detection draws boxes with class labels, which is coarser but faster than a mask
Detection gives a pixel mask, which is finer but slower than boxes
Detection gives one label for the whole image, which is the fastest option
Detection gives a feature vector, which cannot show object position
explain: Segmentation produces a detailed pixel level mask of each object. Detection gives a box and a label, a rougher but quicker result.

q: A team needs the exact shape and boundary of a tumour in a medical scan. Which approach fits best?
options: Object detection with bounding boxes only
Plain classification of the whole scan
A YOLO grid with anchor boxes
Image segmentation, for example with U-Net
explain: Only a pixel level mask shows the exact outline. Boxes are too coarse and a whole image label gives no location at all.

q: A system must find pedestrians and vehicles in video as it plays. Which approach suits this real time task?
options: Image segmentation with a mask for every frame
Object detection, for example with YOLO
Classification with one label for each frame
A bigger classifier that ignores location
explain: Detection gives faster boxes and labels, which suits real time work. A single frame label cannot say where each pedestrian or vehicle is.

q: Why is a one hot label by itself not enough for object detection?
options: The label must also give what is needed to rebuild the bounding box
A one hot vector cannot be compared with the network output
A one hot vector cannot be used with convolutional layers
A one hot vector needs a separate mask image for every class
explain: A one hot vector names the class but says nothing about where the object is. A detection label adds the box centre, width and height.

q: Which items belong in the label an object detector predicts for one object?
options: The centre coordinates of the box
One label that describes the whole image
The class label
The width and height of the box
A full pixel mask of the object
explain: A detection label has at least five values, which are x, y, width, height and class. A pixel mask belongs to segmentation.

q: Why is YOLO described as extremely fast compared with older methods such as Faster R-CNN?
options: It skips the CNN and works on raw pixels directly
It only handles images with a single object in them
It processes the entire image in one forward pass
It labels every pixel before drawing any box
explain: YOLO stands for You Only Look Once, because it looks at the whole image in a single pass. It still uses a CNN and it does not label every pixel.

q: Which steps does an input image go through before the YOLO network uses it?
options: Drawing a pixel mask for each object
Division into an S by S grid
Resizing to a fixed shape
Normalising pixel values to a scale of 0 to 1
Conversion to a single grayscale channel
explain: Images are resized, normalised and split into a grid. Normalising stops large pixel values dominating and helps the network learn faster. Grayscale conversion and masks are not part of it.

q: In YOLO, which grid cell is responsible for detecting a particular object?
options: Every cell that the object touches
The cell that contains the centre of the object
The cell in the top left corner of the image
The cell with the lowest confidence score
explain: Each cell detects objects whose centre falls inside it. This is quicker than checking every possible region as R-CNN does.

q: Which statements about YOLO grid cells are correct?
options: The grid avoids checking every possible region of the image
Each cell predicts several bounding boxes
Each predicted box carries a confidence score
Each cell is responsible for objects whose centre falls inside it
explain: YOLO gives each grid cell the job of detecting objects centred in it and predicts multiple boxes with confidence scores per cell. All four statements are correct.

q: What does the CNN backbone of YOLO, such as Darknet, do?
options: It removes overlapping boxes using intersection over union
It resizes the image to a fixed shape and scales the pixels
It assigns one class label to the entire image
It extracts features such as edges and shapes into a feature map
explain: The backbone is a CNN that builds the feature map from which boxes and classes are predicted. Removing overlaps is the job of non maximum suppression.

q: What does each predicted bounding box in YOLO contain?
options: A pixel mask, a class number and the image resolution
The grid size, the number of anchors and the class count
A centre position, a width and height, and a confidence score
A softmax vector for the whole image and a colour histogram
explain: Each box gives x and y for the centre, w and h for the size, and a probability that an object is present. A pixel mask belongs to segmentation.

q: Why does each YOLO grid cell predict several anchor boxes?
options: Because objects come in different shapes and sizes
Because one box per cell would be too slow to compute
Because anchors replace the need for a CNN backbone
Because anchors are used to normalise the pixel values
explain: A cell may hold a car and a person, which need differently shaped boxes. Several anchors let the model cover varied shapes.

q: How does the way YOLOv3 predicts classes differ from older YOLO versions?
options: It uses softmax instead of sigmoid, so one object can have several classes
It stops predicting classes and only predicts box positions
It predicts one class for each pixel instead of each box
It uses sigmoid instead of softmax, so one object can have several classes
explain: Older versions used softmax so each object received one class. Sigmoid lets several classes apply to the same object, which is useful for multi label problems.

q: Why is non maximum suppression applied to YOLO predictions?
options: The network produces too few boxes for each object
Several boxes can land on one object, so duplicates are removed
Pixel values must be scaled back to the range 0 to 255
The confidence scores must be turned into class labels
explain: Many boxes can land on one object. Non maximum suppression keeps the best box and discards the duplicates so each object appears once.

q: Which steps are part of non maximum suppression?
options: Repeat for the remaining boxes
Keep the box with the highest confidence
Discard remaining boxes that overlap the kept box above the threshold
Sort the boxes by confidence score
Merge all overlapping boxes into a pixel mask
Discard the lowest confidence boxes regardless of overlap
explain: The procedure keeps the most confident box and removes boxes that overlap it too much, then repeats. It is the overlap with the kept box that decides, not confidence alone.

q: In non maximum suppression, what is intersection over union used for?
options: To measure how much one box overlaps another, to spot duplicates
To measure how confident the model is that an object is present
To decide which class an object belongs to
To count how many grid cells the image has
explain: A high overlap with the chosen box shows the box is a duplicate of the same object, so it is removed. Overlap says nothing about class or confidence.

q: Explain the difference between image classification and image segmentation and why segmentation needs different labels.
model: Classification assigns one label to the whole image, which is not enough when the target fills a small area or several objects share the frame. Segmentation assigns a class to each pixel, so it shows where the target is and can find several of them. Because of this the training label must be a binary mask image, not a single category. The network also outputs a prediction mask. Producing the ground truth masks is labour intensive.
points: Classification gives one label for the whole image
Segmentation labels each pixel and so shows where objects are
Training labels must be binary mask images
Ground truth masks are labour intensive to produce

q: Describe the structure of U-Net and say how it produces a segmented image.
model: U-Net turns the image into a feature vector and then rebuilds an image from it, and its layout looks like the letter U. Contraction blocks use convolution layers followed by max pooling to shrink the maps. The bottleneck sits between the two halves. Expansion blocks use convolution layers followed by up sampling to grow the maps again until a segmented prediction mask is produced.
points: Contraction blocks use convolution then max pooling
The bottleneck sits between contraction and expansion
Expansion blocks use convolution then up sampling
The output is a reconstructed segmented image

q: Explain why U-Net uses copy and crop connections.
model: Max pooling in the contraction blocks throws away some spatial information as the maps shrink. Each expansion block therefore receives a copy and crop of the feature maps from the matching contraction block. This hands the lost detail back to the expansion path. It helps the network rebuild a more accurate segmented image than it could from the compressed vector alone.
points: Max pooling loses spatial information
Feature maps are copied from the matching contraction block
The copy hands the lost detail back to the expansion block
The rebuilt mask is more accurate
flag: The last point about accuracy is a reasonable inference. Slide 11 only says copy and crop compensates for information loss.

q: Compare image segmentation and object detection and give one situation where each is the better choice.
model: Segmentation classifies every pixel and gives a detailed mask with the exact shape and boundary of each object. It suits medical imaging and satellite analysis. Object detection draws bounding boxes and gives each a class label. It is coarser but faster, so it suits real time tasks such as finding pedestrians or vehicles. U-Net is a segmentation model, while YOLO is a detection model.
points: Segmentation gives pixel level masks and exact boundaries
Detection gives bounding boxes with class labels
Detection is coarser but faster
Gives one use for each, such as medical imaging for segmentation and vehicle detection for detection

q: Compare the label used for image classification with the label used for object detection.
model: In classification the label is a one hot vector that only says which class the whole image belongs to. In object detection the label must name the class and also hold what is needed to rebuild the bounding box. The model predicts at least five values, which are the box centre x and y, the width and height, and the class label. Detection therefore tells us both what and where.
points: Classification uses a one hot vector for the whole image
Detection needs the class plus box information
Detection predicts at least five values, x, y, width, height and class
Detection says what the object is and where it is

q: Explain how YOLO detects objects in an image, from input to final output.
model: YOLO resizes the image to a fixed shape, normalises the pixels and divides it into a grid. A CNN backbone extracts a feature map. Each grid cell predicts several bounding boxes with a confidence score and predicts class probabilities. Because the whole image is handled in one forward pass, YOLO is fast. Non maximum suppression then removes overlapping duplicates. The final output is a list of boxes, each with a class label and confidence score.
points: The image is resized, normalised and divided into a grid
A CNN backbone extracts a feature map
Each cell predicts boxes, confidence scores and classes
Non maximum suppression removes duplicates
The output is boxes with class labels and confidence scores

q: Explain the role of the grid and anchor boxes in YOLO.
model: YOLO splits the image into an S by S grid and each cell is responsible for objects whose centre falls inside it. This is faster and more efficient than checking every possible region as R-CNN does. Each cell predicts several boxes using anchors, which are boxes of different shapes. Anchors help the model handle objects of varying sizes, for example one anchor suited to a car and another to a person in the same cell.
points: Image is divided into an S by S grid
A cell handles objects whose centre is inside it
The grid is faster than checking every region
Anchors let a cell predict objects of different shapes and sizes

q: Describe how non maximum suppression removes duplicate detections.
model: Several boxes can overlap the same object, so redundant boxes must be removed. All boxes are sorted by confidence score and the one with the highest score is kept. Each remaining box is compared with it using intersection over union. If the overlap is above a threshold, such as 0.5, the box is a duplicate and is discarded. If it is below the threshold the box is kept. The process repeats for the remaining boxes.
points: Many boxes may overlap one object
Sort by confidence and keep the highest
Compare others using intersection over union
Discard those above the threshold and keep those below
Repeat until all boxes are handled

q: Explain how YOLO predicts class labels and how the activation used changed in later versions.
model: After predicting boxes, YOLO outputs a vector of class scores for each detected object, showing how likely each type is, such as car, person or dog. Older versions used softmax, which assigns one class to each object. YOLOv3 and later use sigmoid instead. This allows more than one class prediction for the same object, which helps in multi label classification.
points: Class scores are output for each detected object
Older versions used softmax with one class per object
YOLOv3 and later use sigmoid
Sigmoid allows multiple classes per object
